D.treatment: IHEs with at least 20 TRGP-funded residents
D.comparison: IHEs with fewer than 20 TRGP-funded residents

O.outcome_detail: meeting the suggested cohort-size threshold for economies of scale

cells.quote: Some experts suggest that IHEs need a cohort of around 20 residents to achieve the economies of scale that can help support sustainable and affordable residency programs. This threshold helps IHEs meet minimum class sizes and fund dedicated residency staff. However, even when all self-reported residents are included, regardless of TRGP funding, only 10 of the 24 IHEs with at least one TRGP-funded resident enrolled at least 20 residents.
cells.note: The study reports a descriptive administrative-data comparison against an expert-suggested threshold; it does not measure whether reaching 20 residents actually produced economies of scale.

cells.note: The study reports an observational contrast in engagement during iHelp deployment; no quantitative effect size is printed.

D.treatment: strong instructor promotion, visible online presence, and encouragement of peer help
D.comparison: less instructor promotion, presence, or encouragement

cells.quote: Instructors who strongly promoted the use of the tool, who were visibly present in the online discussions, and who encouraged the peer help model, seemed to engender greater engagement by their students.
cells.note: Observational association from iHelp deployments; the study hedges the finding with “seemed to engender.”

D.comparison: two critical-thinking frameworks and one evidence-based-practice framework

O.outcome_detail: purpose and scope of the frameworks

cells.quote: The purpose of the IHC Framework is similar to that of two frameworks for critical thinking and somewhat similar to that of a framework for evidence-based practice. Those frameworks have broader scopes than the IHC Framework.
cells.note: The study compares framework purposes and scopes rather than learner outcomes; direction is not a better/worse educational effect.

O.outcome_detail: adequacy as a basis for deciding which claims to believe and what to do

cells.quote: An important limitation of broad frameworks is that they do not provide an adequate basis (concepts) for deciding which claims to believe and what to do.
cells.note: The review identifies an advantage of the IHC Framework relative to broad frameworks, but does not report a quantitative effect.

O.outcome_detail: overlap of concepts, competences, and dispositions

cells.quote: There was at most some overlap between the concepts, competences, and dispositions in each of the 22 included frameworks and those in the IHC Framework.
cells.note: The text reports limited overlap, not a comparative learning advantage.

cells.quote: The IHC Key Concepts Framework appears to be unique.
cells.note: This is the review authors' qualitative synthesis conclusion; the study does not define uniqueness as a better/worse outcome.

D.treatment: dry cord care identified as best practice

O.outcome_detail: knowledge-survey response on umbilical cord care

cells.quote: A total of 28% (n = 235) IHCPs responded correctly that the umbilical cord should be allowed to dry to ensure its best care. Slightly more than half of the respondents (51%) answered that they would apply antibiotic powder.
cells.note: Descriptive cross-sectional survey with no instructional treatment or experimentally assigned comparison.

D.comparison: holding the baby by the legs and patting the back

O.outcome_detail: reported response to a neonatal-resuscitation vignette

cells.quote: Given a vignette in which the respondents were to deduce that the baby had poor respiration after birth, 17% (n = 156) correctly identified that they would perform resuscitation using a bag and mask. However, 41% (n = 369) IHCPs incorrectly opted to hold the baby by the legs and pat the back.
cells.note: Cross-sectional knowledge survey; the reported percentages describe different response options rather than an evaluated treatment comparison.
